issues.legal_issue: A constitutional petition may be used to enforce established customary religious rights where the petitioner complains of executive interference, even if the petition also seeks an incidental declaration of those rights.
material_facts: The community claimed customary rights to perform religious ceremonies on specified plots and structures.
Earlier civil-court decisions had adjudicated those customary rights in the community’s favour.
The petition complained that executive authorities had restricted the community’s exercise of those rights.
issues.conclusion: The petition was maintainable insofar as it sought enforcement of established customary rights; the incidental declaration did not make it an impermissible attempt to adjudicate rights for the first time.
issues.legal_principle: Article 32 is ordinarily used to enforce, rather than initially adjudicate, existing or established rights. But where customary rights have already been established and executive interference with them is alleged, the Court must consider the requested enforcement relief on its merits. The rights to practise religion are also protected by Articles 25 and 26 of the Constitution.

predicates.constitutional_rights_enforcement_petiti: A person or group brings a constitutional petition seeking protection of a claimed right.
predicates.established_customary_rights: A competent adjudication or other sufficient prior determination has established the claimed customary rights.
predicates.alleged_executive_interference: The petitioner alleges that executive authorities have deprived or obstructed the exercise of those rights.

issues.definition: When a constitutional petition seeks to protect previously established customary rights from alleged executive interference, the petition is maintainable for enforcement even if it includes an incidental request for a declaration.

issues.legal_issue: A final representative civil-court adjudication of customary religious-use rights binds the represented communities and establishes those rights for later enforcement.
material_facts: A prior representative suit between members of the two religious communities concerned the same plots and structures.
The suit directly put the competing customary rights to use those properties for religious ceremonies in issue.
The final decision rejected the claim of customary rights made by one community and upheld the other community’s entitlement; the decision was affirmed on appeal.
The current petition sought to enforce those rights, except for recitation and utterance of Tabarra.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the community had established customary rights to perform its religious rites, practices, observances, ceremonies and functions on the plots and structures, excluding recitation and utterance of Tabarra.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not exhaustive of the general doctrine of res judicata. The doctrine serves finality of litigation and protects parties from repeated litigation; technical limits of section 11 do not prevent application of the general doctrine when a competent court has decided the relevant issues. The Court relied on Rajah Run Bahadoor Singh v. Musumut Lachoo Koer; Mst. Gulab Bai v. Manphool Bai; Daryao v. State of U.P.; Gulabchand Chhotalal Parikh v. State of Bombay; and Union of India v. Nanak Singh. It also applied Order I Rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure to the representative suit.

predicates.representative_civil_suit: A civil suit is brought by or against representatives of communities after the required representative-proceeding formalities are followed.
predicates.customary_use_rights_directly_in_issue: The suit directly contests the communities’ customary rights to use property for religious purposes.
predicates.competent_court_finally_adjudicated_righ: A court competent to decide the issues gives a final decision on the competing rights.

issues.definition: A final decision in a representative civil suit binds the represented communities when their competing customary religious-use rights were directly in issue and were adjudicated by a competent court.

issues.legal_issue: Final survey findings and registrations of religious endowments under a repealed enactment remain effective under the successor enactment, which permits later registration only of endowments not already registered.
material_facts: A survey report under the earlier enactment listed the properties as endowments of one religious community, and the corresponding notification was published.
No interested person or board brought a challenge within the prescribed period.
The properties were registered under the earlier enactment before its repeal.

The successor enactment preserved the finality of earlier survey findings and treated earlier registrations as registrations under the successor enactment; a later registration was claimed for some properties on behalf of the other community.
issues.conclusion: The earlier survey findings and registrations remained final and effective. The later registration could not displace them, and the Court held the earlier material established the community’s entitlement to its customary rights on the properties concerned.
issues.legal_principle: Under the U.P. Muslim Wakfs Act, 1936, sections 4(5), 5(1)–(3), and 38 provided for survey reports, notification, finality after the time for suit expired, and registration. Under the U.P. Muslim Wakfs Act, 1960, sections 6, 8, 9, 28 and 29 preserved final earlier findings and registrations; “every other Wakf” in section 29 meant a wakf not already registered under the earlier enactment. The Court relied on Board of Muslim Wakfs v. Radha Krishna, while distinguishing the part of that decision concerning a stranger’s paramount title.

predicates.successor_enactment_preserves_prior_find: The later legal scheme continues the effect of final survey findings and registrations made under the earlier scheme.
predicates.prior_survey_report_became_final: A survey report identifying the property as an endowment was not challenged within the applicable time.
predicates.prior_endowment_registration_exists: The property was registered as an endowment under the earlier scheme before that scheme was repealed.

issues.definition: Where the successor scheme preserves final prior findings and registrations, an unchallenged survey finding and an existing earlier registration remain effective.

issues.legal_issue: An order by an executive magistrate restricting conduct to preserve public peace is an executive order amenable to constitutional writ jurisdiction, not a judicial or quasi-judicial adjudication of rights.
material_facts: The challenged restrictions were imposed by an executive magistrate under a preventive public-order power.
The power was exercised to address an apprehended disturbance and preserve public peace, rather than to adjudicate a dispute over rights.
The applicable criminal procedure scheme assigned this public-order function to executive magistrates, while judicial functions were assigned to judicial magistrates.
issues.conclusion: An order made under section 144 of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973 is an executive order and may be challenged under Articles 32 or 226 if it infringes a fundamental right.
issues.legal_principle: The separation of judicial and executive magistrates under the 1973 Code, particularly sections 6, 20–23 and 129–148, places public-order functions, including the function under section 144, with executive magistrates. A hearing and the availability of revision do not convert that function into a judicial one. The Court compared the function with section 37 of the Bombay Police Act, 1951. It distinguished decisions concerning the earlier Code, including Babulal Parate v. State of Maharashtra, K.K. Mishra v. State of Madhya Pradesh and Madhu Limaye v. Sub-Divisional Magistrate, as well as the authorities concerning writs against judicial orders, including Sahibzada Saiyed Muhammed Amirabbas Abbasi v. State of Madhya Bharat, The Parbhani Transport Co-operative Society Ltd. v. Regional Transport Authority, Smt. Ujjam Bai’s case and N.S. Mirajkar’s case.

predicates.preventive_public_order_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a preventive order intended to address an urgent public-order situation.
predicates.order_made_by_executive_magistrate: An executive magistrate makes the challenged order in the performance of an executive public-order function.
predicates.order_does_not_adjudicate_private_rights: The order regulates conduct to preserve public peace without deciding a dispute over the parties’ rights.

issues.definition: A preventive public-order order made by an executive magistrate without adjudicating private rights is an executive act subject to constitutional writ review.

issues.legal_issue: A preventive public-order power must be exercised fairly and, where established legal rights exist, ordinarily in aid of those rights and against those threatening unlawful interference; total suspension of religious rights is a last resort.
material_facts: The community’s customary religious-use rights had been established by prior adjudications and registrations.
Orders had repeatedly restricted or prohibited the community’s ceremonies on grounds of apprehended danger to public peace.
The challenged order prohibited both communities from holding religious discourses and imposed other restrictions.
The community was a religious minority seeking to perform ceremonies protected by its religious faith.
issues.conclusion: The executive magistracy was directed to exercise the preventive power consistently with the stated guidelines, having due regard to established rights and the paramount need to maintain public peace. Total prohibition or suspension of the community’s rights could be used only in an extremely extraordinary situation, as a last measure when other measures would fail.
issues.legal_principle: The preventive power is directed to urgent situations threatening public peace, not to adjudication of civil disputes or title. Established judicially declared rights must be respected and, subject to the paramount public-peace consideration, the power should assist their lawful exercise and be directed against those interfering with it. Where rights are not established, the power should not unfairly give one side a material advantage; legal rights should ordinarily be regulated rather than prohibited. The Court relied on Muthialu Chetti v. Bapun Sahib; Parthasaradi Ayyangar v. Chinna Krishna Ayyangar; Sundram Chetti v. The Queen; Manzur Hasan v. Muhammad Zaman; Haji Mohammad Ismail v. Munshi Barkat Ali; and Madhu Limaye’s case. Articles 25 and 26 inform the protection due to the religious practices of a minority denomination.

predicates.preventive_public_order_proceeding: An executive authority considers a preventive order to address a threat to public peace.
predicates.established_legal_rights: A competent adjudication or other sufficient prior determination has established the rights at stake.
predicates.threatened_interference_with_rights: The authority faces a threat that others will interfere with the lawful exercise of those established rights.

issues.definition: When a preventive public-order proceeding concerns established rights threatened by interference, the power must ordinarily protect their lawful exercise, and total suspension is reserved for an exceptional last resort.

issues.legal_issue: A current representative petition is not barred by res judicata when earlier proceedings involved different parties, did not decide the rights on their merits, or the current proceeding includes the represented communities and additional material.
material_facts: Earlier proceedings had been brought by individuals rather than in a representative capacity for the communities now represented.
The earlier Supreme Court decision did not adjudicate the parties’ rights on their merits but directed them to have their rights adjudicated in a civil suit.
The present petition was brought in a representative capacity, and both relevant endowment boards were joined and heard.
Substantial survey and notification material not produced in the earlier proceedings was before the Court.
issues.conclusion: Neither res judicata nor its analogous principle barred the present petition.
issues.legal_principle: The general doctrine of res judicata is founded on finality and protection from repeated litigation, as explained in Daryao v. State of U.P. The earlier Supreme Court proceedings did not determine the present representative parties’ rights on the merits, and the current proceeding involved different party representation and additional material.

predicates.current_representative_petition: The current proceeding is brought by representatives of the affected community and includes the relevant parties needed for adjudication.
predicates.earlier_proceeding_did_not_decide_rights: The earlier proceeding ended without a merits determination of the rights now asserted.
predicates.parties_are_not_the_same: The earlier proceeding did not involve the same parties in the same representative capacities as the current proceeding.
predicates.substantial_new_material_is_present: The current proceeding contains substantial material that was not before the court in the earlier proceeding.

issues.definition: A current representative petition is not barred when the earlier proceeding did not decide the asserted rights on their merits and the parties differ or substantial new material is presented.

issues.legal_issue: The validity of a preventive order that has expired need not be determined on its merits in a later proceeding, although general guidance may be given for recurring situations.
material_facts: The challenged preventive order restricted religious observances for a particular occasion.
The order had expired by the time the Court considered the challenge.
Similar situations could arise again, and the petitioners alleged that the preventive power had been misused repeatedly.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to determine the expired order’s legality or validity on the merits, but gave general guidelines for future exercises of the power.
issues.legal_principle: Because the particular preventive order had exhausted itself by the passage of time, the Court considered it inappropriate to decide the merits of the challenge to that order. It nevertheless addressed recurring issues by explaining the governing principles for future orders.

predicates.challenge_to_preventive_order: A party asks a court to review a preventive order restricting conduct for a particular occasion.
predicates.challenged_order_has_expired: The challenged order has ceased to operate before the court considers its legality.

issues.definition: When a challenged preventive order has expired before review, its validity is not determined on the merits.
